1.open: Have you ever put off a task you really did not want to do? What did you do instead?
questions: God tells Jonah to "Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh" (v. 2). Nineveh belonged to a feared enemy empire. Why might this have felt like an impossible assignment to Jonah?
Verse 3 says Jonah "got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD." He even paid the fare. What does it look like today when someone runs from what they sense God is asking?

While the storm rages, Jonah has gone down below deck and fallen fast asleep (v. 5). What do you make of a prophet sleeping while everyone else is afraid? When have you gone numb instead of facing something?
The captain has to tell Jonah to "call upon your God" (v. 6). Why is it uncomfortable when someone outside the faith seems more alert than the believer? Has that ever happened to you?

Jonah says, "I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land" (v. 9). How does that line sit beside the fact that he is sailing away from this God? Where do our words and our actions pull apart?

The sailors row hard to save Jonah's life before they give him up, and then they pray, "do not let us perish on account of this man's life" (vv. 13-14). What do these sailors show us about how God can work through people we might overlook?

In the end "the men feared the LORD greatly" (v. 16), and God sends a fish to keep Jonah alive (v. 17). What does this say about how God treats a runaway? If you feel like you have run, or are not sure what you believe, what would you honestly want to say to God about it?
Later in the book Jonah admits he ran because he expected God to show Nineveh mercy. Who are the people we would struggle to want good things for, and why is that harder than facing danger ourselves?
1.life: Ask yourself where you have been quietly dragging your feet on something you sense God is asking of you. This week, take one small, honest step toward it, or tell God plainly why you are afraid.
1.prayer: Thank God that he pursues us even when we run. Ask for honesty about where we are avoiding him, and for a heart that wants good for people we find hard to love.
1.tip: Someone will probably ask whether the great fish is literal. Christians differ on whether Jonah is a historical account or a true-to-life story teaching God's mercy toward outsiders. Say so in a sentence, then steer back to what the chapter shows about running, mercy and the sailors.

2.open: Think of a time you were rescued, even in a small way, like being picked up when your car broke down. What did that feel like?
questions: Jonah prays "from inside the fish" (v. 1). Why do you think he prays now, when he had not prayed while running away? When do people tend to pray?
In verse 2 Jonah says, "In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me." Can you recall a time you called out to God in distress? What happened, or what did you notice afterward?
Jonah says God "cast me into the deep" (v. 3), even though sailors threw him overboard. What do you make of Jonah seeing God's hand in all of this?
In verse 4 Jonah feels "banished from Your sight," yet says he will "look once more toward Your holy temple." What does it look like to turn toward God when you feel far from him?
Verse 7 says, "As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD." What helps you remember God when things feel dark? If remembering feels hard right now, what gets in the way?
Verse 8 says those who "cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion." What are some things people hold onto for safety that cannot actually save them?
Jonah ends with "Salvation is from the LORD!" (v. 9), but he never mentions why he was in the sea. Can a person be truly thankful without facing their own part in the trouble? Why or why not?
Many Christians read Jonah's three days in the fish as a picture of Jesus' death and rising. How does that change the way you hear this prayer, or does it?
2.life: This week, take a few minutes to write your own short prayer in the style of Jonah's: where you have felt low, what God has done, and what you are thankful for. If you can, add one honest line about your own part in a hard situation.
2.prayer: Thank God that he hears us from the lowest places. Ask for the honesty to turn toward him again, and pray for anyone in the group who feels far from him tonight.
2.tip: Readers differ on whether Jonah's prayer shows a real change of heart or mostly grateful relief, since he never mentions his running and later resents God's mercy to others. Say so briefly and don't force a verdict. Let people notice what the prayer includes and leaves out, and keep it gentle so no one feels judged for their own mixed motives.

3.open: Have you ever been given a second chance at something? What was it, and how did it go?
questions: The word of the LORD came to Jonah "a second time" (v. 1). Why do you think God gave Jonah another chance, and what does that tell us about God?
Verse 3 says, "This time Jonah got up and went to Nineveh." Think of a time you finally did something you had been putting off. What changed?
Nineveh was the capital of an enemy empire that later conquered Jonah's own people. How might Jonah have felt walking in with God's message for them?
Jonah's message is only one sentence: "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!" (v. 4). What surprises you about how little he says and how big the response is?
"The Ninevites believed God" (v. 5), from "the greatest of them to the least." What do you notice about who responds, and who might you not expect to respond today?
The king gets up from his throne, takes off his royal robe and sits in ashes (v. 6). What does it cost a powerful person to humble themselves like that?
The king says, "Who knows? God may turn and relent" (v. 9). Have you ever turned back to God without being sure how he would respond? What was that like, or what makes it hard?

Verse 10 says God "saw their actions" and "relented from the disaster." Christians read this in different ways: some see God truly responding to people, others see a warning that was always meant to be conditional. What do you make of that, and how does it shape the way you see God's mercy?
3.life: Think of one person you find hard to forgive or hope well for. This week, pray for them by name once a day, asking God to work in their life and to soften your own heart.
3.prayer: Thank God for giving second chances, to Jonah, to Nineveh and to us. Ask for a heart that is quick to turn toward him and slow to write anyone off.
3.tip: Verse 10 can pull the group into a debate about whether God changes his mind. Name the disagreement in a sentence, then steer back to what the text clearly shows: people turned, and God showed mercy. If someone is quiet, invite them to answer the question about turning back to God with uncertainty, with no pressure to speak.

4.open: Have you ever been really annoyed when someone got off easy, like a friend who got out of a ticket or a kid who got away with something? What happened?
questions: Jonah "was greatly displeased, and he became angry" when God spared Nineveh (v. 1). Why do you think mercy for them felt like a loss to him?

Jonah says he fled because he knew God is "a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion" (v. 2). What is strange about being angry at God for the very things that make God good?
Nineveh was the capital of a empire that would later conquer Israel. What would it have cost Jonah to want good for them? Who might be the Nineveh in our day?

Jonah says, "it is better for me to die than to live" (v. 3). Have you ever been so angry or worn out that you felt like giving up? What does it say that God answers him with a question and not a rebuke?

God asks, "Have you any right to be angry?" (v. 4). Some translations word the question a little differently, for example as a question about whether Jonah is very angry. How does each way of hearing the question change the tone for you?
Jonah was "greatly pleased with the plant" and then furious when it withered (vv. 6-9). What small things tend to shape your mood more than the big things do?

The book ends with God asking whether he should "not care about the great city of Nineveh" (v. 11), and Jonah never answers. How would you answer if you were Jonah? If you are not sure, what makes it hard?

God's concern reaches the people of Nineveh and even "many cattle as well" (v. 11). What does that tell you about how wide God's care is, and how might it change the way you see someone you struggle with?
4.life: Think of one person or group you find it hard to want good for. This week, pray for them by name once a day, even if all you can honestly say is that you want to want what God wants for them.
4.prayer: Thank God that he is "gracious and compassionate," and that we have all needed that mercy. Ask him to soften any place in us that resents his kindness to others.
4.tip: People will likely side with Jonah or find him hard to bear, and Christians read him differently: some as a warning about resenting mercy for enemies, others as a more sympathetic man torn between mercy and justice. Let both views stand, and gently steer back to God's final question, which the group is meant to sit with, not finish neatly.
